A cowl is a loose, hood-like covering — something that drapes, curves, or wraps over something else to cover it. Think of it as a "hood" in the broadest possible sense. This one image — a drooping, curved, protective cover — ties together every meaning of the word.
Meaning 1: A Monk's Hood (or the Whole Robe)

This is the oldest and most classic meaning. A cowl is the large, deep hood attached to a monk's robe. You've seen this in movies: a monk in a long, dark robe with a wide hood that can be pulled up over the head, casting the face in shadow. That hood is the cowl.

Sometimes, the word "cowl" refers to the entire garment — the robe and the hood together — not just the hood alone. So when a medieval monk "put on the cowl," he was putting on his full religious habit.

The cowl in this sense is made of heavy cloth, hangs loosely, and drapes down the back when not worn over the head. It's a defining symbol of monastic life.

The phrase "taking the cowl" means becoming a monk — entering a monastery and adopting that way of life.

"The cowl does not make the monk" is a well-known proverb. It means that wearing the outward symbol of something doesn't make you truly that thing. Just because someone wears a monk's robe doesn't mean they have a monk's virtue. You may recognize this proverb in its Latin form or its equivalent in many languages.

Look at the top of an old chimney or a ventilation shaft, and you'll often see a hood-shaped cap sitting on top of it. That is a chimney cowl.

Its job is practical: it improves airflow up the chimney and prevents wind from blowing back down into the fireplace or flue. Many chimney cowls rotate to always face away from the wind, acting like a weather vane while doing their work. Some look like small spinning turbines; others are simple, fixed metal hoods. But all of them share that same curved, overhanging shape — like a hood sitting on top of a pipe.
Meaning 3: A Cowl in Clothing and Fashion

In modern clothing, "cowl" describes a soft, draped fold of fabric at the neckline of a garment. When a dress or top has a "cowl neck," it means the fabric at the front of the neckline is loose and falls in gentle, cascading folds — like a hood that has been pulled forward and left to hang gracefully. It's an elegant, flowing look.

Separately, a cowl (on its own, as a standalone garment) is a wide, circular loop of knitted or woven fabric worn around the neck. It's like a scarf, but with no ends — just a seamless tube that you slip over your head and wear around your neck and lower face for warmth. Unlike a traditional scarf, it doesn't hang down or get tied. It sits snugly around the neck like a cozy, wide collar.

In aviation and engineering, a cowl — often called a cowling — is the removable cover that fits over an aircraft's engine. It's the smooth, shaped shell that surrounds the engine of a propeller-driven plane, streamlining its shape for aerodynamics and protecting the engine from wind and debris. When a mechanic needs to work on the engine, they open or remove the cowling.

More broadly, in cars and machinery, a cowl can refer to any protective hood-shaped cover over mechanical components — including the area on a car between the base of the windshield and the engine compartment.

When something has a cowl — or resembles one — it can be described as cowled.

  • A cowled figure is a person wearing a hood (often used in literature and film to create a mysterious, shadowy character).
  • A cowled chimney has a cowl on top of it.
  • A cowled engine is one fitted with a cowling.

Every use of the word "cowl" comes back to the same physical idea: a curved, drooping, hood-like form that covers or wraps over something. Whether it's a monk's hood, a chimney cap, a draped neckline, or an engine cover — each one shares that same quality of being a protective, overhanging covering shaped like a hood. Once you hold that image in your mind, every meaning of the word will feel natural and connected.
